report.source_text: Within 4 days, the patient was noted to have severe weakness of the left upper extremity and neuropathic pain in the left hand and forearm. Neurology was consulted. On examination, tone was absent in the left hand, wrist and elbow. The left biceps reflex was reduced with absence of the left brachioradialis and triceps reflexes. Pin and thermal sensation were absent over the entire left forearm and hand, with presence of tactile allodynia. Strength was reduced as follows: biceps 2/5, triceps 0/5, wrist and finger extensors 0/5, wrist and finger flexors 3/5, forearm pronation 3/5, forearm supination 2/5, superficial and deep finger flexors 3/5 and intrinsic hand muscles 3/5. The left deltoid, infraspinatus and pectoral muscles were strong at 5/5. There was no scapular winging (table 1).

clinician.request: What were the detailed findings on electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction studies (NCS) of the left upper extremity? Specifically, which nerve(s) showed abnormalities and what was the pattern (demyelination, axonal loss, conduction block)?

The proposed mechanism is COVID-19-induced hypercoagulability causing microthrombi in vasa nervorum of the brachial plexus. report.source_text: NCS revealed markedly reduced left median and ulnar compound muscle action potential response amplitudes with slowing of motor conduction velocities due to axon loss. The left-sided median, ulnar, radial, musculocutaneous and medial antebrachial cutaneous responses were all absent. Needle EMG of muscles in the left upper extremity showed fibrillations and positive sharp waves in all muscles except the deltoid, where examination was normal. Recruitment was absent in the left triceps, brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis, extensor digitorum communis and extensor indicis. Recruitment was reduced in the remaining assessed muscles.

report.source_text: On examination of the left upper extremity, tone was no longer absent but was reduced across the left wrist. The left triceps and forearm showed severe muscle atrophy without fasciculations. Tendon reflexes were absent in the left arm. There was reduced pin and thermal sensation in the left C5-T1 dermatomes with absent vibration to the left elbow and absent proprioception to the left wrist. Strength was reduced as follows: triceps 4/5, wrist and finger extensors 0/5, wrist and finger flexors 4/5, forearm supination 4/5 and intrinsic hand muscles 4-/5 (table 1).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 52-year-old man with hypertension and newly diagnosed diabetes presented to the ED in March 2020 after 4 days of cough, shortness of breath, fatigue, and myalgias. He was febrile (38.6°C), tachycardic, tachypneic, and hypoxic (90% on room air) with bilateral multifocal pneumonia on chest X-ray. SARS-CoV-2 was confirmed by RT-PCR. By day 28 of illness, he developed severe left upper extremity weakness with neuropathic pain in the left hand and forearm. Neurologic examination revealed absent tone in the left hand, wrist, and elbow; reduced/absent reflexes (biceps reduced, brachioradialis and triceps absent); absent pin and thermal sensation over the left forearm and hand with tactile allodynia; and weakness pattern consistent with brachial plexus injury (C5-T1 distribution): biceps 2/5, triceps 0/5, wrist/finger extensors 0/5, with sparing of deltoid, infraspinatus, and pectorals (5/5). EMG/NCS at day 49 showed axonal loss pattern with markedly reduced median and ulnar compound muscle action potential amplitudes, absent sensory responses (median, ulnar, radial, musculocutaneous, medial antebrachial cutaneous), and denervation (fibrillations and positive sharp waves) in all left upper extremity muscles except deltoid. MRI of the left brachial plexus revealed T2 hyperintensity and thickening of the entire brachial plexus without contrast enhancement, plus acute denervation edema of the left serratus anterior. Laboratory studies showed elevated Factor VIII activity (184%; reference 50-150%) and mildly reduced protein S activity (65%; reference 75-125%), supporting a hypercoagulable state. At 3 months post-discharge, the patient showed partial recovery with persistent weakness and sensory loss in the C5-T1 distribution.
